## What you will do

In Notebook 1 you interviewed a handful of finfluencer twins. This notebook
works with the full panel: about 90 twins of real financial influencers on X,
each interviewed every trading day and asked to rate 100 large US stocks from 0
(a very strong sell) to 100 (a very strong buy). You will:

1. **aggregate:** turn each day's answers into one number per stock, a
   *signal* saying how bullish the twins are on it that day;
2. **match:** line each signal up with what the stock did *afterwards*, relative
   to the S&P 500;
3. **backtest:** sort the stocks on the signal every day, and ask whether the
   ones the twins liked beat the ones they didn't;
4. **score forecasts:** look at a second task, where the same kind of twins gave
   probabilities for economic events traded on Polymarket, and compare them with
   the market price and with what happened;
5. **watch twins deliberate:** replay one stored session in which ten twins
   argued for four rounds before agreeing on one stock to buy.

Nothing here calls a language model. The interviews have already been run and
are loaded from files, so the notebook runs offline in a few seconds.

**How to read this notebook.** As in Workshop 1, every table and figure the
code prints has a number, given in bold just above the code that prints it, and
the text says which table, row or column a number comes from.

The first block loads the R packages the notebook uses and sets the folders it
reads from and writes to.

```{r libs}
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

DATA <- file.path("..", "data")
OUT  <- file.path("..", "output")
dir.create(OUT, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

---

## 1. Inputs

The block below loads the twins' answers, already added up by stock and day, as
a table called `panel`, and prints its size and span.

**Table 2.1.** `panel`: rows, trading days, stocks and twins per day.

```{r panel}
panel <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ff_signal_panel.csv"))
panel[, event_date := as.IDate(event_date)]
data.table(rows = nrow(panel),
           days = uniqueN(panel$event_date),
           first_day = min(panel$event_date),
           last_day  = max(panel$event_date),
           stocks = uniqueN(panel$ticker),
           median_twins_per_row = median(panel$n_twins))
```

Each row of `panel` is one stock on one trading day. Its columns summarise what
the twins said about that stock that day:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n_twins` | twins who rated the stock that day |
| `mean_rec` | their average rating, 0–100 |
| `sd_rec` | how much they disagreed: the standard deviation of the ratings |
| `buy_share` | share of twins rating it 65 or more (a buy) |
| `sell_share` | share rating it 35 or less (a sell) |
| `net_buy_share` | `buy_share − sell_share`: from −1 (all sell) to +1 (all buy) |
| `mean_conf` | their average confidence in the rating, 0–100 |

Two details of how a day is defined, both settled before the file was written.
A twin interviewed after 15:30 New York time counts towards the *next* trading
day, because by then the market has nearly closed and the twin's view could only
be acted on the following day. And if a twin was interviewed twice on one day,
only the later interview counts.

The block below prints the first five rows so you can see the columns filled in.

**Table 2.2.** `panel`: the first five rows.

```{r panel-head}
head(panel, 5)
```

The second file holds the stocks' returns. For every stock and trading day it
has the day's **log excess return**: the stock's log return from the previous
close to this close, minus the S&P 500's. A positive number means the stock beat
the market that day. Log returns add up over days, which is why the file uses
them. The returns are computed from Yahoo Finance adjusted closing prices.

**Table 2.3.** `rets`: rows, stocks and span.

```{r returns}
rets <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ff_excess_returns.csv"))
rets[, date := as.IDate(date)]
data.table(rows = nrow(rets), stocks = uniqueN(rets$ticker),
           first_day = min(rets$date), last_day = max(rets$date))
```

The returns run about two weeks past the last interview day in Table 2.1, so
even the last signals can be followed for ten trading days.

---

## 2. From answers to a signal

A **signal** is one number per stock and day that ranks the stocks from most to
least favoured. `panel` offers several; this notebook uses `net_buy_share`, the
one used in the Talking to Machines finfluencer research, and Exercise 2.1 asks
you to try `mean_rec` instead.

The block below takes the last interview day in the panel and prints the five
stocks the twins were most bullish on and the five they were most bearish on.

**Table 2.4.** The most and least favoured stocks on the last day.

```{r top-bottom}
last_day <- max(panel$event_date)
day <- panel[event_date == last_day][order(-net_buy_share)]
rbind(cbind(group = "most favoured",  head(day, 5)[, .(ticker, net_buy_share, mean_rec, sd_rec)]),
      cbind(group = "least favoured", tail(day, 5)[, .(ticker, net_buy_share, mean_rec, sd_rec)]))
```

Notice in Table 2.4 that even the "least favoured" stocks often have a
`net_buy_share` above zero. The twins are bullish on most stocks most of the
time. What matters
for a signal is the *ranking* on a given day, not the level. That is why the
backtest below compares stocks with each other on the same day.

---

## 3. Matching signals to later returns

A signal on day *t* can only be judged on what happens *after* it. The twin
answered before 15:30 on day *t*, so the earliest you could trade on it is the
close of day *t*. The block below adds, for every stock and day, the log excess
return over the next *h* trading days: the sum of the daily returns on days
*t*+1 to *t*+*h*. It does this for *h* = 1, 5 and 10.

```{r forward}
setorder(rets, ticker, date)
for (h in c(1L, 5L, 10L)) {
  col <- paste0("fwd_", h, "d")
  rets[, (col) := Reduce(`+`, lapply(seq_len(h), function(k)
                    shift(log_excess_ret, k, type = "lead"))), by = ticker]
}
```

The block below joins those forward returns onto `panel` by stock and day, as a
table called `events`, and prints how many stock-days have a forward return at
each horizon.

**Table 2.5.** `events`: stock-days with a forward return, by horizon.

```{r join}
events <- merge(panel, rets[, .(ticker, event_date = date, fwd_1d, fwd_5d, fwd_10d)],
                by = c("ticker", "event_date"))
events[, .(with_1d = sum(!is.na(fwd_1d)), with_5d = sum(!is.na(fwd_5d)),
           with_10d = sum(!is.na(fwd_10d)))]
```

---

## 4. The backtest

The test is simple. Every day, sort that day's stocks on `net_buy_share` into
five equal groups, **quintiles**: quintile 1 holds the fifth the twins liked
least, quintile 5 the fifth they liked most. Then average the forward excess
return within each quintile, day by day. If the twins know something, quintile 5
should beat quintile 1. The difference, quintile 5 minus quintile 1, is the
return of a **long–short** portfolio: buy the favoured fifth, short the
disfavoured fifth, so the market's own movement cancels out.

The block below assigns the quintiles. Ties are broken at random, with a fixed
seed so everyone gets the same answer.

```{r quintiles}
set.seed(13)
events[, quintile := ceiling(5 * frank(net_buy_share, ties.method = "random") / .N),
       by = event_date]
```

The block below averages the forward return in each quintile on each day, then
across days, and prints it in basis points (1 bp = 0.01 percentage points).

**Table 2.6.** Mean forward excess return by quintile (bp), averaged over days.

```{r by-quintile}
q_day <- events[, .(fwd_1d = mean(fwd_1d, na.rm = TRUE), fwd_5d = mean(fwd_5d, na.rm = TRUE),
                    fwd_10d = mean(fwd_10d, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(event_date, quintile)]
q_tab <- q_day[, lapply(.SD, function(x) round(1e4 * mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), 1)),
               by = quintile, .SDcols = c("fwd_1d", "fwd_5d", "fwd_10d")][order(quintile)]
q_tab
```

Figure 2.1 shows the same thing over time: for each quintile, the average
cumulative excess return from the day of the signal (day 0) to ten trading days
later. The block below computes it for every horizon from 1 to 10 and plots it.

**Figure 2.1.** Cumulative excess return after the signal, by quintile.

```{r path, fig.height = 4.5}
path <- rbindlist(lapply(1:10, function(h) {
  r <- copy(rets)[, fwd := Reduce(`+`, lapply(seq_len(h), function(k)
                     shift(log_excess_ret, k, type = "lead"))), by = ticker]
  e <- merge(events[, .(ticker, event_date, quintile)],
             r[, .(ticker, event_date = date, fwd)], by = c("ticker", "event_date"))
  e[, .(bp = 1e4 * mean(fwd, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(event_date, quintile)][
    , .(bp = mean(bp, na.rm = TRUE)), by = quintile][, h := h]
}))
path <- rbind(data.table(quintile = 1:5, bp = 0, h = 0L), path)
ggplot(path, aes(h, bp, colour = factor(quintile), group = quintile)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "RdYlGn", name = "Quintile\n(5 = most favoured)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(x = "Trading days after the signal", y = "Cumulative excess return (bp)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The block below computes the long–short return day by day, quintile 5 minus
quintile 1, and summarises it: its average, its t-statistic (the average
divided by its standard error), and the share of days on which it was positive.

**Table 2.7.** The long–short portfolio (quintile 5 minus quintile 1).

```{r long-short}
ls <- dcast(q_day, event_date ~ quintile, value.var = c("fwd_1d", "fwd_5d", "fwd_10d"))
ls_tab <- rbindlist(lapply(c("1d", "5d", "10d"), function(h) {
  s <- ls[[paste0("fwd_", h, "_5")]] - ls[[paste0("fwd_", h, "_1")]]
  s <- s[is.finite(s)]
  data.table(horizon = h, days = length(s), mean_bp = round(1e4 * mean(s), 1),
             t_stat = round(mean(s) / (sd(s) / sqrt(length(s))), 2),
             share_positive = round(mean(s > 0), 2))
}))
ls_tab
```

**How to read Table 2.7.** Row `1d`, column `mean_bp` is what the long–short
portfolio earned over the day after the signal, on average across the days in
column `days`. Rows `5d` and `10d` hold the positions longer. A t-statistic
around 2 or more is the usual bar for "unlikely to be luck".

Two cautions before you read too much into it:

- **The window is short.** `r ls_tab[horizon == "1d", days]` days (Table 2.7,
  column `days`) is a few months of one market. The same test on a longer
  window, or a different one, can come out differently.
- **The 5- and 10-day t-statistics are too generous.** Consecutive days' 10-day
  returns share nine of their ten days, so they are not independent, and the
  simple standard error above understates the uncertainty. Exercise 2.2 asks you
  to fix this.

---

## 5. Prediction markets

The twins were also asked about the economy. On 21 April 2026, `r uniqueN(fread(file.path(DATA, "ff_prediction_markets.csv"))$twin_id)`
twins gave a probability for each of 17 events traded on **Polymarket**, a
prediction market. Examples: "the Fed makes no change at its June 2026 meeting",
"unemployment reaches 5.0% at some point in 2026". Each question showed the twin
the event's Polymarket price that day. A price of 0.93 means traders, together,
put the chance at about 93%.

By mid-August 2026, 9 of the 17 events had settled. The block below loads the
file as `pm` and prints, for each settled event, the twins' average probability,
the Polymarket price they were shown, and the outcome (1 = it happened).

**Table 2.8.** Settled events: twins' average probability, market price, outcome.

```{r pm}
pm <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ff_prediction_markets.csv"))
settled <- pm[!is.na(outcome)]
settled[, .(twins_mean = round(mean(twin_prob, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            market_price = round(market_prob[1], 2), outcome = outcome[1]),
        by = .(code, question)]
```

Two rows of Table 2.8 have no `market_price`: the twins were not shown one for
those questions.

A standard score for probability forecasts is the **Brier score**: the average
of (probability − outcome)², where the outcome is 0 or 1. Zero is perfect;
always saying 0.5 scores 0.25. Lower is better. The block below scores three
forecasters on the settled events that had a market price: the individual twins,
the twins' average (the "crowd"), and the market price itself.

**Table 2.9.** Brier scores on the settled events with a market price (lower is better).

```{r brier}
s <- settled[!is.na(market_prob) & !is.na(twin_prob)]
crowd <- s[, .(p = mean(twin_prob), m = market_prob[1], o = outcome[1]), by = code]
data.table(forecaster = c("individual twins", "twin crowd (average)", "market price"),
           events = uniqueN(s$code),
           brier = round(c(mean((s$twin_prob - s$outcome)^2),
                           mean((crowd$p - crowd$o)^2),
                           mean((crowd$m - crowd$o)^2)), 3))
```

In Table 2.9 the twin crowd (`twin crowd (average)` row, 0.237) scores a little
better than the typical single twin (`individual twins` row, 0.248): averaging
cancels some of each twin's own noise. Both are close to the 0.25 of always
saying 0.5, and both are worse than the market price (`market price` row, 0.191).

Figure 2.2 shows each twin's probability (a dot) against the market price it was
shown (the black bar), for every settled event with a price, with the outcome in
the panel title.

**Figure 2.2.** Twins' probabilities against the market price, settled events.

```{r pm-fig, fig.height = 5}
s[, label := sprintf("%s (outcome %d)", code, outcome)]
ggplot(s, aes(x = twin_prob, y = label)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, width = 0, alpha = 0.35, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(aes(x = market_prob), shape = 124, size = 7) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Probability", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**What this can and cannot show.** The twins were *shown* the market price, so
this is not an independent forecast set against the market: it asks how far the
twins move away from a number they were given, and whether moving away helped.
Look at Figure 2.2 for where the twins spread widely around the bar and where
they sit on it. And with one interview day and seven events, Table 2.9 is a
description, not a test.

---

## 6. Twins that talk to each other

Every twin so far answered alone. Talking to Machines also runs a second design
every trading day: ten finfluencer twins discuss the day's market in short,
tweet-length posts, over four rounds, and the stock most of them back at the end
is bought. This section replays one stored session, from 28 September 2026. No
model is called. The ten agents are a different set of finfluencers from
Notebook 1 and are renamed Agent A to Agent J; the posts are theirs, with names
and hashtags removed.

The block below loads the posts as `posts`, one row per agent and round, and the
session's settings as `session`, and prints the settings.

**Table 2.10.** The deliberation session of 28 September 2026.

```{r delib}
posts   <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ff_deliberation_posts.csv"))
session <- jsonlite::fromJSON(file.path(DATA, "ff_deliberation_session.json"))
data.table(date = session$date, model = session$model, agents = session$n_agents,
           rounds = session$rounds, minutes = session$minutes, cost_usd = session$cost_usd)
```

The model in Table 2.10 is not the `gpt-5-mini` of the daily panel: this design
was built separately, on `gpt-4.1-mini`.

The rules change from round to round. In round 0 each agent posts blind, seeing
nobody else. In rounds 1 and 2 each agent is shown posts written before its
turn (the columns `sees_this_round` and `sees_total` count them) and gets the
instruction below. The block prints it word for word.

**Text 2.1.** The instruction for rounds 1 and 2.

```{r delib-rule, comment = ""}
wrap <- function(x) cat(unlist(lapply(strsplit(x, "
")[[1]], function(l)
  if (nzchar(l)) strwrap(l, 80, exdent = if (startsWith(l, "- ")) 2 else 0) else "")), sep = "
")
wrap(session$instructions$round_1)
```

The final round replaces it with the instruction below.

**Text 2.2.** The instruction for round 3, the last.

```{r delib-final, comment = ""}
wrap(session$instructions$round_3)
```

The block below puts each agent's buy pick side by side across the rounds. The
`contrarian` agent was the session's designated devil's advocate: told to push
back on whatever consensus formed and, in the last round, to pick a different
stock if five or more others were backing the same one, unless that stock was
genuinely the best choice.

**Table 2.11.** Each agent's buy pick, by round.

```{r delib-picks}
dcast(posts, agent + style + contrarian ~ paste0("round_", round), value.var = "buy_ticker")
```

The block below counts the agents behind each stock in each round.

**Table 2.12.** Number of agents picking each stock to buy, by round.

```{r delib-counts}
counts <- dcast(posts, buy_ticker ~ paste0("round_", round), fun.aggregate = length,
                value.var = "agent")
counts[order(-round_3, -round_0)]
```

Figure 2.3 draws Table 2.11 as a grid, one colour per stock, so the drift is
easy to follow.

**Figure 2.3.** Buy picks by agent and round.

```{r delib-fig, fig.height = 4.5}
ggplot(posts, aes(x = factor(round), y = agent, fill = buy_ticker)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = buy_ticker), size = 3.2) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(x = "Round", y = NULL, fill = "Buy pick") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

In Table 2.12, no agent picks AMAT in round 0 (`round_0` column, AMAT row); by
round 3, eight of the ten do. The block below prints the first two posts that
name AMAT, with how many posts each agent had seen before writing.

**Text 2.3.** Where AMAT came from.

```{r delib-amat, comment = ""}
show_posts <- function(d) for (i in seq_len(nrow(d)))
  cat(sprintf("Round %d, %s (had seen %d posts), buys %s:", d$round[i], d$agent[i],
              d$sees_total[i], d$buy_ticker[i]),
      strwrap(d$text[i], 76, indent = 2, exdent = 2), "", sep = "
")
show_posts(posts[grepl("AMAT", text)][1:2])
```

The block below prints the posts that cite the anti-herding rule of Text 2.1.

**Text 2.4.** Agents applying the rule.

```{r delib-rule-cited, comment = ""}
show_posts(posts[grepl("anti-herding", text, ignore.case = TRUE)])
```

At the end, another call to the model reads the whole discussion and writes a
summary. The block below prints its verdict on what the discussion added.

**Text 2.5.** The session's own verdict.

```{r delib-verdict, comment = ""}
wrap(session$summary$value_added)
```

**What this can and cannot show.** Text 2.5 credits the discussion with
"mitigating herd risk", yet in Table 2.12 the group ends on the one stock a
single agent brought up in round 1 (Text 2.3), and later posts repeat that
agent's argument. Part of the result is the design: the rule in Text 2.1 pushes
agents off the stocks three others have named (Text 2.4 shows them saying so),
and Text 2.2 tells them to agree. Even Agent G, the devil's advocate, ends on
AMAT (Table 2.11, `round_3` column). Change the rules and a different stock may
win. This is one session on one day, and whether buying AMAT paid off is not
assessed here.

## Exercises

**Exercise 2.1 — another signal.** Re-run the quintile sort of Section 4 with
`mean_rec` instead of `net_buy_share`. Does the long–short return in Table 2.7
change? Why might a share of buy votes and an average rating rank stocks
differently?

**Exercise 2.2 — honest standard errors.** The 5- and 10-day rows of Table 2.7
use overlapping returns. Recompute them using only every 5th (or 10th) day, so
that no two holding periods overlap. How do `mean_bp` and `t_stat` change?

**Exercise 2.3 — disagreement.** Split the stock-days by `sd_rec` at its median.
Is the signal stronger when the twins agree, or when they disagree?

**Exercise 2.4 — moving off the price.** In `pm`, for each settled event with a
market price, compute how far the twin crowd sat from the price
(`mean(twin_prob) − market_prob`). Were the twins right more often when they
moved away from the market, or when they stayed close?

**Exercise 2.5 — the sell side.** Repeat Table 2.12 with `sell_ticker` in place
of `buy_ticker`. What happens to MU, which three agents wanted to buy in round 0?

**Exercise 2.6 — did the rule bind?** Five agents picked AVGO in round 0 (Table
2.12). In Table 2.11, which of them still pick it in round 1, and which agents
move *to* AVGO in round 1? Is that what the rule in Text 2.1 asks for?

The block below saves `events` to `output/`, for your own use after the workshop.

```{r save}
fwrite(events, file.path(OUT, "ff_events.csv"))
```
